answer.label: Written by

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Book III (“The Modern Worker”), Chapter XI, “Labour”

source.excerpt: Blessed is he who has found his work; let him ask no other blessedness. He has a work, a life-purpose; he has found it, and will follow it! How, as a free-flowing channel, dug and torn by noble force through the sour mud-swamp of one’s existence, like an ever-deepening river there, it runs and flows… Labour is Life.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the line to Carlyle’s Past and Present (1843), chapter “Labour,” and records no attribution dispute.
The exact wording appears in the Project Gutenberg full text of Past and Present, in Book III, Chapter XI.
WIST Quotations gives the same citation — Book 3, Ch. 11, “Labour,” 1843.
source.excerptNote: From the chapter “Labour.” The famous opening sentence is followed by Carlyle’s river-through-the-swamp image and the linked aphorism “Labour is Life.”

author.name: Thomas Carlyle
author.heading: About Thomas Carlyle
author.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish-born writer and one of the most influential social critics of Victorian Britain. His 1843 polemic Past and Present contrasted the disciplined life of a medieval monastery with the spiritual emptiness he saw in industrial England, and it made the “gospel of work” central to his thought. Lines from its chapter “Labour” — including this one — became touchstones of the Victorian work ethic.

misattribution.heading: Setting the record straight
misattribution.intro: This one is unusual for a “magnet” name: the attribution is correct. The quote is often passed around with no source or as an anonymous proverb, but it is genuinely Carlyle’s and appears verbatim in his work.

items.why: The line circulates on quote sites and inspirational posters detached from any source, which nudges people to treat it as a folk saying. It is not — it is a specific sentence Carlyle wrote in the “Labour” chapter of Past and Present.

misattribution.truthLine: The exact wording is Carlyle’s, printed in Past and Present (1843) and preserved in the Project Gutenberg full text; Quote Investigator records no rival claimant.

context.heading: Why it endured
lead: Carlyle wrote Past and Present during the “Hungry Forties,” a period of economic distress and unrest in Britain. Against that backdrop he preached that meaningful labour was itself a form of salvation — and this sentence is the compressed heart of that argument.

The full passage extends the thought with a vivid image: honest work runs through a life “like an ever-deepening river,” draining a “sour mud-swamp” into “a green fruitful meadow,” before Carlyle distils it to three words: “Labour is Life.”
